newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH TV PREMIERA TO CHANGE NAME, PROGRAMME - AGENCY.
newsitem.headline: CZECH TV PREMIERA TO CHANGE NAME, PROGRAMME - AGENCY.

text.p: Czech private television station Premiera TV a.s. on Monday said it would change its name and launch a new programming schedule before the end of this year, the local news agency CTK reported.
CTK quoted Premiera's Director Milos Petana as saying that the new name and logo, introduced due to complaints from foreign channels using the same name, would be revealed on October 15.
"It will have a new name, logo, jingles, design, scheme, programme structure," CTK quoted Petana as saying.
Officials at the station were not immediately available for comment.
Premiera, currently transmitting to 27 percent of the country, or 58 percent of its population, will also extend its network of transmittors, the agency said.

The station is 47 percent-owned by broadcasting licence holder FTV Premiera, fully owned by Czech bank IPB , which also holds 14 percent directly. Stratton Investments of Bahamas-based investor Michael Dingman holds 15 percent.
Insurer Ceska Pojistovna holds 10 percent directly and 14 percent through its investment arm Kapitalova Investicni Spolecnost.

Petana added that shareholders of Premiera were ready to invest into the project in order to turn the company into a lucrative business, after three years of muddling through with a tiny viewership, and only a 4.7 percent market share.
Premiera already changed its programming structure once this year and replaced general director Jiri Mejstrik with Petana, who is also the station's chairman.

The station faces fierce competition with TV Nova, majority owned by New York cosmetics heir Ronald Lauder's Central European Media Enterprises Group, which has taken a 70 percent market share since launching the former East Bloc's first state-wide commercial TV station in early 1994.

Nova has captured the lion's share of advertising in the 10 billion crown per year Czech TV market with a steady diet of mostly American-generated action films, soap operas, detective serials, and sitcoms, and sensational news programming.
Premiera, meanwhile, has been unable to crack the market, with its mixture of dated European fare mixed with older American serials.
